title: The Dangerous Seduction of Clarity
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Andrea Chiarelli, writing with foresight strategist Cecile Cremer, argues that our habit of prizing clear, focused questions can quietly keep teams and leaders stuck. They define 'wrong questions' as those that feel speculative, awkward or out of place, but that expose assumptions the usual framing hides. A neat survey item like 'how satisfied are you with your provider' already decides what matters, so clarity narrows the lens even as it feels rigorous. The piece offers a short guide to asking wrong questions well, through unsettling but coherent framing, metaphor and taboo, and room for futures that do not yet exist. It also names the limits: such questions need psychological safety and good timing, and work best early in framing rather than mid-decision. It ends with a challenge to ask one wrong question this week.
points: Clear, tidy questions embed hidden assumptions about what matters, so clarity can narrow thinking even as it signals rigour.
Wrong questions are valuable because they break linear, polite thinking and surface assumptions people did not know they were making.
Good wrong questions create productive tension rather than confusion, for example by asking which reason for failure the team would least want to admit.
Metaphor, taboo and paradox pull people out of operational mode into reflective mode.
These questions need psychological safety and the right moment; in a tense room or at decision time they will land flat.
quotes: We’re taught to pursue certainty. Clear questions, clear answers, clear decisions. This signals rigour, professionalism and a steady hand.

These are ‘wrong’ questions. Not because they’re illogical, but because they violate an unspoken rule. They break the rhythm of polite, linear thinking. And that disruption is exactly what makes them powerful.

It sounds rigorous. But, beneath the surface, it’s already decided what matters. It assumes satisfaction is the right metric. That the provider is the right unit of analysis. So you can see how clarity can quietly narrow the lens.
Sometimes, the most valuable question does not fit neatly on a Likert scale. It’s the one that forces us to ask: “What’s missing from how we’re framing this?
Wrong questions often work best when they borrow language from somewhere else: narrative, moral, emotional, even poetic. They pull us out of operational mode and into reflective mode.
If you’re mid-decision, or if the room is already tense, dropping “What if none of this matters?” won’t help. Wrong questions need the right conditions: curiosity, psychological safety, timing.

If your culture sees questions as signs of weakness or delays, you’ll need to do some groundwork first. And readiness is both emotional and cognitive: if the context can’t handle doubt, even the best question will land flat. That’s simply a signal about the system, and not necessarily an issue with the question itself!
